Empirical Research Plan:  “The Effect of Living Near a Registered Sex Offender on Residential Property Values”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Primary strategy:  Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study
panel built from repeat sales.

Why DID is appropriate
• We observe the same property (or a very small neighborhood cell) before and after the date on which a nearby sex offender’s address becomes publicly posted.  
• Properties just outside the immediate radius (e.g., 0.10–0.25 miles) provide a credible counterfactual: they share the same micro-neighborhood price trends but are not “treated.”  
• The registry’s public disclosure date is arguably exogenous to individual houses’ price paths, creating a plausibly quasi-experimental shock to the information set of buyers.

Supplementary robustness:  a local spatial RDD at a sharp 0.10-mile cutoff
(street-network distance) and an IV that instruments “treatment” with the interaction of (i) pre-registry offender residence and (ii) the date the web registry goes live.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment indicator (Treat_it)  
= 1 if property i is sold t months after the earliest date on which a registered sex offender’s published address sits within 0.10 miles (528 ft) along the street network.

Control group  
Properties whose nearest offender is 0.10–0.25 miles away at sale t.  
Rationale: very similar micro-location but perceived risk is far lower once the radius exceeds a short walk.

Event timing  
For each offender residence j, define τ_j  = official date the address first appears on the public registry (or, if only move-in date is known, the move-in date).  
For a sale at time t we build POST_it = 1{t ≥ τ_j} when the offender is within 0.10 m.

Running variable & cutoff for RDD (robustness)  
Running variable: network distance in feet to nearest offender.  
Cutoff: 528 ft (0.10 miles).  Houses on either side of that threshold are compared within a ±1 000 ft bandwidth.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends. In the absence of disclosure, prices of houses ≤0.10 miles and 0.10–0.25 miles from the offender would have evolved similarly.  Plausibility:  they are literally next-door blocks; we can test with pre-period event-study coefficients.

A2. No strategic anticipation.  Sellers/buyers did not learn the offender’s location before the public posting (or at least not differentially by radius).  Megan’s Law required sudden disclosure, making anticipation less likely.

A3. Stable composition & no interference.  Treatment of one house does not change the counterfactual trend for control houses that lie just outside 0.10 m.  Spillovers may exist but should be tiny at that distance; we will check via placebo rings.

A4. Offender location exogenous to *future* neighborhood price growth.  Because addresses are often court-mandated and low-income rental availability drives location, forward-looking price shocks are unlikely to determine offender siting.

A5. Data accuracy.  Offender address and posting dates are correctly measured.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Endogenous offender siting: Offenders may choose downward-trending neighborhoods.  
   • Include very granular fixed effects: property FE (repeat-sales) or 100 × 100 m grid-cell FE × year.  
   • Event-study pre-trend test: coefficients on leads (k < 0) should be ≈ 0.

T2. Differential neighborhood shocks (e.g., new school, plant closure) within 0.25 miles.  
   • Include census-block-group-by-year FE and tract-specific time trends.  
   • Limit sample to sales taking place within ±3 years of disclosure to shorten horizon.

T3. Spatial spillovers contaminate control ring.  
   • Redo analysis with alternative control rings (0.15–0.30 miles, 0.20–0.40 miles).  
   • Supplement with RDD which estimates the limit from the left and right of the 0.10-mile boundary.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# --- 0. Packages ------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(sf)             # spatial operations / network distances pre-computed
library(fixest)         # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(did)            # event-study robust to staggered treatment
library(rdrobust)       # RDD

# --- 1. Data ----------------------------------------------------------
sales <- fread("nc_property_sales_1994_2004.csv")     # one row per sale
off   <- fread("nc_offender_addresses.csv")           # offender id, addr, post_date

# assume network distances pre-computed and merged:
# dist_ft: distance in feet to nearest offender address at time of sale
# nearest_off_post: posting date of that nearest offender (NA if >0.25 mi)

# --- 2. Variable construction ----------------------------------------
sales[, treat_radius := fifelse(dist_ft <= 528, 1L, 0L)]
sales[, control_radius := fifelse(dist_ft > 528 & dist_ft <= 1320, 1L, 0L)]

# POST indicator relative to offender posting date
sales[, post := sale_date >= nearest_off_post]

# main DID treatment dummy
sales[, TreatPost := treat_radius * post]

# log price
sales[, lprice := log(sale_price)]

# --- 3. Main DID specification ---------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(lprice ~ TreatPost + bedrooms + baths + sqft +
                  i(year) | property_id + bg_year,
                  data = sales[ treat_radius==1 | control_radius==1 ],
                  cluster = "bg_year")   # bg_year = block-group × yr

summary(did_main)

# --- 4. Event study with did2s ---------------------------------------
event_dt <- sales[ treat_radius==1 | control_radius==1 ]
event_dt[, rel_time := as.integer(floor((sale_date - nearest_off_post)/365.25))]
event_est <- feols(lprice ~ i(rel_time, ref = -1) | property_id + bg_year,
                   data = event_dt[abs(rel_time)<=5], cluster = "bg_year")
iplot(event_est)    # visualize leads and lags

# --- 5. Spatial RDD robustness ---------------------------------------
rdd_dt <- sales[dist_ft <= 2000]   # 2k ft bandwidth
rdd_dt[, running := dist_ft - 528]  # distance from cutoff
rd <- rdrobust(y = rdd_dt$lprice, x = rdd_dt$running, c = 0,
               covs = rdd_dt[,.(bedrooms,baths,sqft)])
summary(rd)
```

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Prior:  Proximity to a registered sex offender lowers sale prices.  
Magnitude:  −4 % to −8 % for properties within 0.10 miles relative to similar houses 0.10–0.25 miles away, based on capitalization of perceived crime risk and the elasticity seen for other neighborhood disamenities (landfills, crime hot-spots).

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
C1. Pre-treatment parallel trends tested and satisfied ………………… 1  
C2. No anticipatory behavior ………………………………………………………… 0.8  
C3. Stable composition / no selective migration affecting control … 0.7  
C4. No interference between units within chosen ring ……………… 0.7  
C5. Correct specification & robustness (alt. rings, RDD) ………… 1  

Average ≈ 0.84 → overall credible but not bullet-proof; most concern rests on spatial spillovers and unobserved offender siting motives, which are partially but not fully addressable.
